subject: Accounting
title: Audit Committees
description: A quick, practical guide to Audit Committees.

hook.text: The audit committee is the board's financial watchdog. It meets privately with auditors.

buildup.text: Audit committees oversee financial reporting, internal controls, and the external audit process.

discovery.text: Post-SOX rules require all audit committee members to be independent—no management ties.

twist.text: At least one member must be a financial expert. In practice, many committees lack deep expertise.

climax.text: A strong audit committee gives auditors a safe channel to raise concerns without management blocking them.

punchline.text: The audit committee is where auditors can speak freely.

quiz.question: What must audit committee members be after Sarbanes-Oxley?

details.summary: Audit committees are independent board subcommittees that oversee financial reporting, internal controls, and external audits. This topic explores their role in protecting investors and maintaining trust in corporate financial statements.
details.whyItMatters: Audit committees act as a check on management, ensuring financial reports are accurate and auditors remain independent. Weak audit committees have been linked to major corporate scandals.
takeaways: Audit committees must include independent directors with financial expertise
They oversee external auditors and can hire or fire the audit firm
Post-Enron reforms made audit committees legally responsible for oversight

faq.question: What does an audit committee do?
faq.answer: An audit committee oversees a company's financial reporting process, monitors internal controls, manages the relationship with external auditors, and ensures compliance with laws and regulations to protect shareholder interests.

faq.question: Why are independent audit committee members required?
faq.answer: Independence ensures committee members can challenge management without conflicts of interest. Sarbanes-Oxley requires public companies to have fully independent audit committees to prevent the kind of failures seen in Enron and WorldCom.
